text.en: Meena saw a river carve a valley in a picture. "Rivers cut rock!" she said.

Exogenetic (external) processes work from outside on the surface. Weathering breaks down or changes rock in place. Temperature changes, water and living things can all contribute. Erosion removes material. Rivers, wind, glaciers and waves can then transport it and deposit it in another place.
Rivers form V-shaped valleys, waterfalls, meanders, flood plains and deltas. Glaciers carve U-shaped valleys, wind makes dunes in deserts and waves make cliffs, caves and beaches.
These processes reshape landscapes over time. Rivers can leave fresh deposits on flood plains, while erosion can remove useful topsoil.

Compare a cracked rock with the loose pieces at the bottom of its slope. The crack shows weathering. The pieces on the slope show that some material has moved.

board.text: Rock breaks in place · loose material moves

text.en: In physical weathering, a rock splits into smaller pieces while the minerals keep their chemical identity.
Water that enters a crack can freeze and expand. Repeated freezing and thawing can widen the crack over time.

board.text: Freeze and thaw can widen cracks

text.en: Some rounded rocks shed curved outer layers. This peeling of sheets is called exfoliation.
In chemical weathering, minerals change or dissolve. Oxygen reacting with minerals that contain iron can form reddish or brown iron oxides.
Rainwater can dissolve carbon dioxide to form a weak acid. Over time that water can dissolve some limestone through joints and openings.

board.text: Weakly acidic water can dissolve limestone

text.en: Growing roots can widen existing cracks. Organisms can also release substances that change minerals. Both are ways living things contribute to weathering.

board.text: Living things act physically or chemically

text.en: In mass movement, gravity pulls soil and rock downslope. Creep is very slow. A landslide can move a mass of material much more quickly.
After heavy rain, water can weaken a slope and make movement more likely. Slope material and steepness also matter.

board.text: Rainfall is one contributor to slope movement

text.en: Gradation includes the lowering of some surfaces and the building up of others. A stream can cut down into one place and leave sediment farther along.
A fast stream on a steep slope can cut into its bed. Valleys with narrow bottoms and sloping sides often have a V-shaped cross-section.
Rock layers may wear away at different rates. A resistant ledge above a weaker layer can help a waterfall develop.

board.text: Contrasting rock resistance can form a waterfall

text.en: Some grains roll or bounce along the riverbed. Finer grains can stay suspended in moving water, and dissolved material travels with the water itself.

board.text: Bed load · suspended load · dissolved material

text.en: In a meander, erosion is common at the outer bank and sediment builds up on the inner bank. The difference can shift the bend over time.

board.text: Outer bank erodes · inner bank builds

text.en: If a river cuts across the narrow neck of a meander, the old loop may become separated. Water trapped in it can form an oxbow lake.
Floodwater spreads across low land beside a river. As it slows, it can leave layers of fine material and build up a flood plain.

board.text: Floodwater deposits sediment across low land

text.en: Where a river enters a lake or sea, deposition can build a delta if enough sediment accumulates. Strong waves and currents can carry some sediment away.
Groundwater moving through limestone can enlarge passages into caves. Where mineral-bearing water drips, it can leave deposits that grow from the roof or floor.

board.text: Cave roof · stalactite · cave floor · stalagmite

text.en: A moving glacier can scrape and remove rock along its bed. This can deepen and widen a valley into a broad U-shaped trough.
A glacier can carry particles of different sizes and leave a ridge of debris called a moraine. The ridge can record a former edge of the ice.

board.text: Moraine · a ridge of debris left by ice

text.en: Wind can lift loose fine particles. Sand grains blown against rock can wear its surface by abrasion.

board.text: Wind can remove particles and abrade rock

text.en: Windblown sand can pile into dunes, often where air flow slows or sand collects. Fine windblown silt can settle over much larger areas.
Waves can exploit cracks and cut into a headland, sometimes forming caves and arches. Sediment spread by waves and currents can build beaches elsewhere.

board.text: Waves reshape exposed rock and move sediment

text.en: To explain a landform, look for evidence of the agent and process. A cut bank points to erosion. Layers of sand at a river mouth suggest deposition.

board.text: Identify the agent · interpret the evidence

problem.en: A stream cuts into its outer bank and a strip of sand builds on the inside of the same bend. Identify the process on each side.

text.en: Locate where material is being removed.

why.en: The outer bank loses sediment as the river erodes it.

text.en: Locate where new material accumulates.

why.en: The river deposits sand on the inner bank as the flow slows.

prompt.en: A friend says Weathering and erosion are the same. How will you reply?

points.en: Weathering changes or breaks down rock in place. Gravity drives mass movement down slopes.
Rivers, glaciers, wind, waves shape land.
